content: Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) is a rare condition that follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. It is one of the leading causes of death in infants, particularly those aged between one month and one year, in the United States. In 1830, Kopp proposed the concept of thymic asthma, suggesting that an enlarged thymus might lead to the death of a child. During the 18th century, other theories emerged, attributing sudden infant deaths to mechanisms such as asphyxia, suffocation, catarrh, superstitions, or even the actions of witches and gods. In 1969, Horgan introduced the term sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). By 1971, SIDS was officially recognized as a diagnosis on death certificates and included in the WHO International Classification of Diseases. In 1982, Kelly and colleagues were the first to identify apneic episodes in newborn siblings of infants who had died from SIDS. In 1986, Bass and colleagues reported cases of accidental asphyxiation in infants caused by objects in the crib or violent shaking, which could lead to a severe condition known as shaken baby syndrome. That same year, Smialek collected data on twin infants who died suddenly and simultaneously. In 1990, the Back to Sleep program was introduced, leading to a significant reduction in SIDS cases. In 1992, Filiano and Kinney were the first to report an association between developmental hypoplasia of the arcuate nucleus and the occurrence of SIDS. The Wear and Tear hypothesis posits that sudden infant death may result from painful, stressful, or traumatic exposures experienced in utero, which overwhelm the neonatal regulatory systems that are incompatible with maintaining allostasis.
